newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon's Hariri heads for third term as premier.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon's Hariri heads for third term as premier.

text.p: Billionaire tycoon Rafik al-Hariri headed on Wednesday for a third successive term as Lebanon's prime minister after MPs consulted by President Elias Hrawi overwhelmingly backed his reappointment.
All but one of the first 45 deputies or representatives of parliamentary groups who met Hrawi by early afternoon said they wanted Hariri to head the new cabinet.

Hrawi must nominate the choice of the majority of the 128 deputies. Political sources said he would name the new prime minister on Thursday, before French President Jacques Chirac arrives in Beirut on a Middle East tour.
Hrawi is scheduled to complete his meetings with deputies by one p.m. (1100 GMT) on Thursday, several hours before Chirac's arrival in the evening.
He began seeking the deputies' opinions after talks on Tuesday with Syrian President Hafez al-Assad in Damascus, whose 35,000 troops in Lebanon make him the country's main power broker.
Hariri and his 29-member cabinet resigned last week to allow a new government to be formed after recent parliamentary elections. They have stayed on in a caretaker capacity.
Political sources expect the new government -- which must receive a parliamentary vote of confidence -- to be sworn in by the end of October or early November.

Hariri, who has headed two cabinets since October 1992, is expected to have greater influence in parliament thanks to resounding victories scored by supporters of his Syrian-backed government in the elections.
He won his first parliamentary seat and will head a bloc of about 20 deputies, one of the biggest in parliament. He had few supporters in the previous parliament.
This is expected to facilitate approval of projects in Hariri's multi-billion plan to rebuild Lebanon that were blocked by the previous parliament.

Despite working to strengthen the Lebanese currency and boost international confidence in postwar Lebanon, Hariri has been accused of sinking the country into debt by borrowing on the international markets to finance rebuilding.
Critics also say he has no social policy taking into account the situation of the poor but he has said the new government must give top priority to social policy.
